newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South African business sees stability returning.
newsitem.headline: South African business sees stability returning.

text.p: A small rise in South Africa's August Business Confidence Index (BCI) is a sign the economy is stabilizing, the South African Chamber of Business (SACOB) said on Thursday.
But SACOB director-general Raymond Parsons told a news conference the economy was still vulnerable to jolts.

"The increase provides an indication that stability is returning to South Africa and that the relatively positive fundamentals are starting to re-assert themselves...(however) business confidence still remains vulnerable to shock," he said.
The August BCI rose 0.4 percent from July to 117.0. The gain follows a 2.3-percentage point drop in July from June's 118.9.

Parsons said positive sentiment stemmed from the announcement of new steps to cut crime, the fact an interest rate rise seemed to have been avoided, the solid second-quarter gross domestic product data and the slight recovery in the rand.
Parsons said there was no doubt South Africa would meet its target of three percent growth this year.
"Nothing can happen now between now and the end of the year to take that away from us," he said. The economy grew by 3.3 percent in 1995.
The BCI data also pointed to a soft-landing for the economy, Parosns said.
"We are not talking about a recession. We are talking about a levelling off this year as all the evidence points to a soft-landing for the South African economy," he said.
Parsons also suggested there was some scope for an interest rate cut if the economy slowed too much later in the year.
Earlier this year, finance minister Trevor Manuel announced the government's macroeconomic plan aimed at creating annual growth of six percent and 400,000 new jobs a year by 2000.
Parsons called on the government to move faster on privatisation, one of the plan's key planks, if the scheme was to reap its intended economic goals.
"If we go about privatisation in a dynamic and pro-active way, it will facilitate the government's task in meeting those targets," he said.

He said a successful plan would stave off the sort of shocks SACOB warned that the economy was still vulnerable to. "(The plan) is the best shock-absorber we could wish for as far as the South African economy is concerned," Parons said.

The only gloomy news came in SACOB's separate survey of confidence in the manufacturing sector. Keith Lockwood, SACOB economist, predicted the sector would not see any increse in employment this year, barring big direct foreign investment.
"I would be very doubtful that we are going to see any net gains in employment in the formal manufacturing sector,' Lockwood said.
